title: The Secret Account Behind Your Birth Certificate

scenes.purpose: Open on the size of the bill the homeowner sent her bank.

visual.description: One large tile: the bill's amount counts up and lands as the narration says it; the label 'Bill of exchange' sits beneath.

chart.title: Her payment
chart.note: One plaintiff's bill, as described in her complaint; not a typical amount.

scenes.direction: Cold open; the figure lands on 'two hundred forty-four thousand'.
scenes.narration: A homeowner sent the bank holding her mortgage a bill of exchange for $244,663.79, drawn, she said, on a trust account run through the IRS.

scenes.purpose: Her conclusion in her own words.

visual.description: Quote card; the words appear as spoken, 'paid off' turns amber.
onScreenText: "this loan is paid off"

citations.label: Plaintiff's complaint, Bryant v. Washington Mutual

scenes.direction: Hold half a second after the last word.
scenes.narration: She argued that once the bank received it, "this loan is paid off".

scenes.purpose: Pose the question the video answers.

visual.description: The question types on, large and centred; 'secret Treasury account' holds in amber.
onScreenText: Is there really a secret Treasury account in your name?

scenes.direction: Type on with the narration; beat after the question mark.
scenes.narration: Is there really a secret Treasury account in your name that can pay off your debts?

scenes.purpose: Name the real things the story points at, so the viewer sees why it sounds checkable.

visual.description: Three lines build one per cue as each is spoken: birth certificate, Treasury, commercial code.
onScreenText: Your birth certificate
The Treasury
The commercial code

scenes.direction: Each line appears on its word.
scenes.narration: The story behind her bill points at real things, your birth certificate, the Treasury, the commercial code, so every step sounds like something you could check.

scenes.purpose: Step one of the story, the strawman, in a promoter's words.

visual.description: Quote card; 'corporate fiction' turns amber as spoken.
onScreenText: "The all capitals spelling of the name creates a corporate fiction"

scenes.narration: It starts with your name in capital letters. The site jonhoyle.com says "The all capitals spelling of the name creates a corporate fiction", which believers call the strawman.

scenes.purpose: Step two, the birth certificate as a traded bond.

visual.description: Quote card; 'being traded' turns amber as spoken.
onScreenText: "These birth certificate bonds have a value and are being traded"

scenes.narration: Next comes your birth certificate, which the site Understand Contract Law treats as an investment: "These birth certificate bonds have a value and are being traded".

scenes.purpose: Step three, the account you can draw on.

visual.description: Quote card; 'can be drawn from' turns amber as spoken.
onScreenText: "there is an alphanumeric account number in your Strawman name that is your private account that can be drawn from"

scenes.narration: And the value is supposed to sit in an account you can reach: jonhoyle.com says "there is an alphanumeric account number in your Strawman name that is your private account that can be drawn from".

scenes.purpose: Step four, the stamp that supposedly opens the account.

visual.description: Quote card; 'your treasury account' turns amber as spoken.
onScreenText: "what's going to give you access into your treasury account"

scenes.narration: The way in is a stamp: in one YouTube how-to video, a red stamp with your Social Security number on a bill is "what's going to give you access into your treasury account".

scenes.purpose: The kit is sold, and the Treasury says nobody has profited from it.

visual.description: Quote card; 'No one has profited' turns amber as spoken.
onScreenText: "No one has profited from the Treasury Department by using these tactics"

scenes.direction: Hold a beat after the quote.
scenes.narration: The kit is for sale: the Treasury notes that some websites sell videos, webinars and coaching on how to do this, and that "No one has profited from the Treasury Department by using these tactics".

scenes.purpose: Turn to the evidence, starting with the account.

visual.description: The question types on as 'Does it exist?' is spoken.
onScreenText: Does the account exist?

scenes.narration: So start with the account itself. Does it exist?

scenes.purpose: Show the Treasury's own words that the accounts do not exist.

visual.description: The Treasury notice passage; the highlight sweeps across the sentence as it is read.

excerpt.highlight: these accounts are fictitious and do not exist in the Treasury system

scenes.narration: The Treasury says these accounts "are fictitious and do not exist in the Treasury system".

scenes.purpose: The Sixth Circuit and the IRS agree there is no such account.

visual.description: The IRS passage quoting United States v. Anderson; the highlight lands on the IRS's 'pure fantasy' line as the second sentence is spoken.

excerpt.highlight: The notion of secret accounts assigned to each citizen is pure fantasy

citations.label: IRS, The Truth About Frivolous Tax Arguments (citing US v. Anderson, 6th Cir.)

scenes.direction: Highlight on 'pure fantasy'; hold a beat.
scenes.narration: A federal appeals court, the Sixth Circuit, said the same: the Treasury "does not maintain depository accounts against which an individual can draw a check, draft, or any other financial instrument". The IRS puts it more bluntly: "The notion of secret accounts assigned to each citizen is pure fantasy".

scenes.purpose: Turn to the birth certificate.

visual.description: The question types on.
onScreenText: What about the birth certificate?

scenes.narration: What about the birth certificate that is meant to fill it?

scenes.purpose: The Treasury: a birth certificate has no money value.

visual.description: Quote card; 'no monetary value' turns amber as spoken.
onScreenText: "There is no monetary value to a birth certificate"

scenes.narration: The Treasury's answer: "There is no monetary value to a birth certificate", and a birth certificate cannot be used to buy anything.

scenes.purpose: A court rejects the birth certificate as a contract.

visual.description: The Gravatt opinion passage; the highlight sweeps the line about birth certificates and contractual rights as it is read.

excerpt.highlight: recognize or impose contractual rights, obligations, or duties

scenes.narration: In Gravatt v. United States, a man told the Court of Federal Claims that his birth certificate was a contract with the United States, and the court called that frivolous: birth certificates, it said, do not "recognize or impose contractual rights, obligations, or duties".

scenes.purpose: The same court on the trust fund.

visual.description: Quote card; 'strains all logic and reason' turns amber as spoken.
onScreenText: "strains all logic and reason to believe that the trust fund alleged by plaintiff actually exists"

scenes.narration: He also claimed to be owed money from a trust fund held in the Treasury, and the court wrote that it "strains all logic and reason to believe that the trust fund alleged by plaintiff actually exists".

scenes.purpose: The strawman has no basis in law in three countries.

visual.description: Two quote lines appear as spoken, the Canadian history first, the Queensland court second, each with its own citation.
onScreenText: "has no basis in law in either the US or Canada"
"does not find any reflection in any provision of our law"

citations.label: Netolitzky, history of OPCA in Canada
Supreme Court of Queensland, via Hobbs, Young and McIntyre

scenes.direction: Second line on 'in Australia'; hold a beat.
scenes.narration: And the strawman itself? A history of these movements in Canada says it "has no basis in law in either the US or Canada", and in Australia the Supreme Court of Queensland found that the idea "does not find any reflection in any provision of our law".

scenes.purpose: Turn to the stamped bill.

visual.description: One large title.
onScreenText: The stamped bill

scenes.narration: That leaves the stamped bill.

scenes.purpose: The Treasury calls the bills worthless and fraudulent.

visual.description: The Treasury notice; the highlight sweeps 'All these Bills of Exchange drawn on the U.S. Treasury are worthless' as it is read.

excerpt.highlight: All these Bills of Exchange drawn on the U.S. Treasury are worthless

citations.label: US Treasury, bogus sight drafts notice

scenes.narration: The Treasury says "All these Bills of Exchange drawn on the U.S. Treasury are worthless", and that drawing such drafts on it "is fraudulent and a violation of federal law".

scenes.purpose: A Canadian court on the same strategy.

visual.description: Lines build as spoken: the lender, the bonds, the court's finding; 'frivolous and illogical' in amber.
onScreenText: Farm Credit Canada
Bonds on secret Treasury accounts
Frivolous and illogical

citations.label: New Brunswick Court of Appeal, via Netolitzky and Warman

scenes.narration: In Canada, a family whose wood lots were financed by Farm Credit Canada said they had paid with bonds drawn on secret accounts run by the US Treasury; the New Brunswick Court of Appeal found the strategy frivolous and illogical, and said the family knew this.

scenes.purpose: What happened to the homeowner.

visual.description: The Bryant opinion; the highlight sweeps 'did not tender payment, but rather a worthless piece of paper' as the judge's words are spoken.

excerpt.highlight: did not tender payment, but rather a worthless piece of paper

scenes.direction: Highlight on 'worthless piece of paper'; hold a beat.
scenes.narration: As for the homeowner, the bank told her the bill was an unacceptable form of payment, and went on to foreclose on her home. When she sued, the federal judge found that she "did not tender payment, but rather a worthless piece of paper", while accepting that her belief in the process seemed genuine.

scenes.purpose: Passing the bills has led to criminal convictions.

visual.description: Two lines build one per sentence: the promoter's conviction, then the Heath conviction upheld.
onScreenText: Barton Buhtz: convicted of fraud
United States v. Heath: conviction upheld

citations.label: IRS, The Truth About Frivolous Tax Arguments (US v. Heath, 6th Cir.)

scenes.direction: Second line on 'United States v. Heath'.
scenes.narration: The man whose redemption advice she had followed, Barton Buhtz, had just been convicted in Oregon, with several co-defendants, of fraud charges for passing bills of exchange. Sending one can be a crime by itself: in United States v. Heath, the Sixth Circuit upheld a conviction for presenting a fictitious financial instrument, a "Registered Bill of Exchange" sent to the IRS with no actual account behind it.

scenes.purpose: Say plainly what the sources do not count.

visual.description: One title line, muted colour, no emphasis.
onScreenText: How often ordinary users are charged: not counted

citations.label: IRS, The Truth About Frivolous Tax Arguments

scenes.narration: How often an ordinary user ends up charged, none of these sources counts; what they record are the convictions of a promoter and of people who passed the bills.

scenes.purpose: The first answer.

visual.description: One large title; 'No' lands on the spoken 'no'.
onScreenText: First answer: no

citations.label: US Treasury, bogus sight drafts notice

scenes.direction: Punch in on 'no'; hold a beat.
scenes.narration: So the answer to the first question is no: the Treasury says the account does not exist, and the courts in this evidence that looked at these bills treated them as worthless.

scenes.purpose: Bridge to the second question.

visual.description: Split-field wipe from the account question to the gold question.

scenes.narration: With the account gone, the promoters fall back on the idea underneath it: that ever since the country left gold, no debt can truly be paid at all.

scenes.purpose: The 1933 claim in promoters' words.

visual.description: Two quote lines, one per sentence, each with its own citation; 'pay their debts' and 'discharge' turn amber.
onScreenText: "As a result of HJR 192, the people can no longer pay their debts."
"eliminated our ability to pay our debts allowing only for their discharge"

citations.label: Take Back Your Strawman Birth Certificate Bonds, YouTube

scenes.narration: The site Educated in Law states it in one line: "As a result of HJR 192, the people can no longer pay their debts." A video called Take Back Your Strawman Birth Certificate Bonds says the change "eliminated our ability to pay our debts allowing only for their discharge".

scenes.purpose: Ask what the law says.

visual.description: The question types on.
onScreenText: What does that resolution actually say?

scenes.direction: Type on; beat after the question mark.
scenes.narration: So what does that resolution actually say?

scenes.purpose: Read the 1933 resolution from the judge's opinion.

visual.description: The Bryant passage on House Joint Resolution 192; the highlight sweeps the heading as it is read.

excerpt.highlight: To assure uniform value to the coins and currencies of the United States

citations.label: H.J. Res. 192 (1933), quoted in Bryant v. Washington Mutual

scenes.narration: The judge in that mortgage case read it, and it is a real law from 1933, headed "To assure uniform value to the coins and currencies of the United States". It made contract clauses demanding payment in gold against public policy, and it declared US currency "legal tender for all debts".

scenes.purpose: The Supreme Court on what the resolution meant.

visual.description: Quote card; 'dollar for dollar' turns amber as spoken.
onScreenText: "actual number of dollars promised, dollar for dollar"

citations.label: Guaranty Trust Co. v. Henwood (1939), quoted in Bryant

scenes.narration: A 1939 ruling the homeowner also cited, Guaranty Trust Co. v. Henwood, explained what Congress wanted: a debt in dollars is measured by the "actual number of dollars promised, dollar for dollar".

scenes.purpose: The judge: the law is only about leaving gold.

visual.description: Quote card; 'away from the gold standard' turns amber as spoken.
onScreenText: "nothing more than the U.S. monetary shift away from the gold standard"

scenes.direction: Hold a beat after the quote.
scenes.narration: Nothing in it mentions secret trust accounts or bills of exchange, the judge wrote; it addresses "nothing more than the U.S. monetary shift away from the gold standard".

scenes.purpose: Federal Reserve notes are legal tender.

visual.description: The IRS passage on legal tender; the highlight sweeps 'Congress has declared federal reserve notes legal tender' as it is read.

excerpt.highlight: Congress has declared federal reserve notes legal tender

citations.label: IRS, The Truth About Frivolous Tax Arguments (US v. Rifen; US v. Condo)

scenes.narration: The notes in your wallet count too: as one federal appeals court put it, "Congress has declared federal reserve notes legal tender". In a tax case, the Ninth Circuit rejected as "frivolous" the argument that Federal Reserve Notes "are not valid currency, cannot be taxed, and are merely" debts.

scenes.purpose: The second answer.

visual.description: One large title; 'No' lands on the spoken 'no'.
onScreenText: Second answer: no

citations.label: IRS, The Truth About Frivolous Tax Arguments

scenes.direction: Punch in on 'no'; hold a beat.
scenes.narration: So the answer to the second question is no: leaving gold changed what backs a dollar, not whether a dollar pays a debt.

scenes.purpose: Tie both answers to 1933.

visual.description: One large title; '1933' in amber.
onScreenText: Both answers meet in 1933

citations.label: US Treasury, bogus sight drafts notice

scenes.narration: Both answers meet in the same place: the Treasury says the scheme's story starts with 1933, and the 1933 law says the opposite of what that story needs.

scenes.purpose: What the viewer should do.

visual.description: Two lines build one per sentence: the lender's response, then the question to ask the seller.
onScreenText: No payment at all
Ask for one court that accepted it

scenes.direction: Second line on 'ask'; hold two seconds at the end.
scenes.narration: So if a way to pay needs you to believe the Treasury is hiding your money, expect your lender to treat it as no payment at all. And before you stamp anything, ask whoever is selling the method for one court that accepted it.
